entry: Family of southern frogs with 206 species in 13 genera, distributed throughout [[Mexico]], the [[Caribbean]], and Central and [[South America]]. The name comes from Greek, meaning a bird or other animal having slender toes. The family most likely diverged from other hyloids during the [[Cretaceous]]. Its members are terrestrial, burrowing, aquatic, and arboreal, and inhabit a wide range of habitats. Several genera lay their eggs in foam nests placed in crevices, on water surfaces, or on forest floors, and these nests are among the most varied of any frogs. When eggs hatch in forest-floor nests, the [[Tadpole|tadpoles]] remain within the nest, without eating, until [[Metamorphosis|metamorphosis]]. Recent revisions moved the former subfamily Eleutherodactylinae into its own family, Eleutherodactylidae. Fossils have been found in Maastrichtian India.

Class of elementary particles with half-integer spin that do not undergo the [[Strong interaction|strong interaction]]. There are two main classes: charged leptons, including the [[Electron|electron]], muon, and tau, and neutrinos, which are electrically neutral and rarely interact with other matter. Charged leptons combine with other particles to form atoms. Six leptons, known as flavors, are grouped in three generations: the electron and its neutrino, the muon and its neutrino, and the tau and its neutrino. Electrons have the least mass of the charged leptons. Muons and taus decay rapidly into electrons and neutrinos, so electrons are the most common charged lepton in the universe. All leptons are subject to gravitation, the [[Weak interaction|weak interaction]], and electromagnetism. The electron was discovered in 1897 by [[J. J. Thomson]], and the muon was discovered in 1936 by Carl D. Anderson. The term was introduced by Léon Rosenfeld in 1948.

Large oil painting by Spanish artist [[Pablo Picasso]], created in 1907 and held by the [[Museum of Modern Art]]. It shows five nude female prostitutes in a brothel on Carrer d'Avinyó in Barcelona, with angular, disjointed bodies. The far-left figure has Egyptian or southern Asian features, the two adjacent figures an Iberian style, and the two on the right African mask-like features. Picasso rejected Renaissance perspective in favor of a compressed picture plane, making the work a precursor of [[Cubism]]. Deemed immoral at its first exhibition in 1916, it angered even Picasso's closest associates. [[Henri Matisse]] considered it a bad joke, yet indirectly reacted to it in his 1908 *Bathers with a Turtle*. Georges Braque initially disliked it but studied it closely, and his collaboration with Picasso led to Cubism. Poet André Salmon gave it its current title when it was shown publicly, replacing Picasso's *Le Bordel d'Avignon*.

Epic historical novel by [[Victor Hugo]], first published on March 31, 1862. It is considered one of the greatest novels of the 19th century and has been adapted for film, television, and the stage, including as a [[Les Misérables (musical)|musical]]. Beginning in 1815 and culminating in the June Rebellion of 1832 in Paris, it follows ex-convict Jean Valjean, whose character is loosely based on Eugène François Vidocq, through his redemption and his pursuit by the police inspector Javert. The novel examines the nature of law and grace, the [[History of France|history of France]], the architecture and urban design of Paris, politics, moral philosophy, justice, religion, and romantic and familial love. Hugo drew on incidents he witnessed, including the 1846 arrest of a bread thief. English-language alternatives to the title include *The Wretched* and *The Dispossessed*.

Sung-through musical based on [[Victor Hugo]]'s novel *Les Misérables*. Conceived in the late 1970s by French librettist Alain Boublil, with music by Claude-Michel Schönberg, the original French version was recorded as a concept album in 1980. An English-language version, adapted by Cameron Mackintosh and directors Trevor Nunn and John Caird, opened in London in 1985 to mixed reviews but great success with audiences. It has run continuously in London since then, the longest-running musical in West End history. It is one of the highest-grossing stage musicals of all time, and a film adaptation was released in 2012.

Homosexual woman or girl. The word derives from the Greek island of [[Lesbos]], home of the poet [[Sappho]], some of whose surviving poetry expresses her love for other women. The earliest mentions of lesbianism date to around the 600s–500s BC. The idea of a lesbian as a category of person distinct from other women emerged in Europe around the turn of the 19th century. Modern polls estimate that 1 to 2% of women are lesbian. Lesbians' rights vary widely worldwide, from severe persecution to legal protection. Social movements advocate anti-discrimination protections, child custody protections, and legal civil unions or marriage.

Greek island in the northeastern [[Aegean Sea]] (pop., 2021: 83,755). It covers 1,633 sq km (631 sq mi), the third-largest island in Greece and the eighth-largest in the Mediterranean. In Homer's [[Iliad]], Lesbos was part of the kingdom of Priam, which ruled from [[Troy]]. It was under Byzantine and Genoese rule in the Middle Ages, and the [[Ottoman Empire]] conquered it in 1462. The Ottomans ruled until the First Balkan War in 1912, when it became part of the Kingdom of Greece. Sometimes called the Island of the Poets, it was home to [[Sappho]] and Alcaeus.

Canadian-American actor and comedian known for deadpan comedy. Born in [[Regina, Saskatchewan]], he worked for 60 years, appearing in more than 100 films and 150 television programs. He first gained standing as a dramatic actor in films such as *Forbidden Planet* (1956). After *Airplane!* (1980), he became known for comedy, and critic [[Roger Ebert]] called him "the Olivier of spoofs." He starred in the *Naked Gun* film series, based on the short-lived television series *Police Squad!* (1982). He was inducted into both Canada's Walk of Fame and the [[Hollywood Walk of Fame]], and was made an Officer of the Order of Canada in 2001.

Landlocked kingdom in [[Southern Africa]], surrounded by [[South Africa]] (pop., 2024: 2.23 million). Its capital and largest city is Maseru. It was formed in 1824 by King Moshoeshoe I, became a British protectorate in 1868, and was a crown colony from 1884. It gained independence in 1966. Constitutional government was restored in 1993 after seven years of military rule. The Sotho people make up 99.7% of the population, and the country takes its name from them. Lesotho is a [[Constitutional monarchy|constitutional monarchy]], headed by King Letsie III, son of Moshoeshoe II. Subsistence agriculture, textile exports, diamond mining, and water sales support an economy in which high poverty affects nearly half the population. Lesotho is a member of the [[United Nations]], the [[African Union]], and the [[Commonwealth of Nations]], and its literacy rate of 81% as of 2021 is among the highest in Africa.

Archipelago at the eastern edge of the [[Caribbean Sea]], forming part of the West Indies. The islands form an arc from the Virgin Islands southeast through the Leeward and Windward Islands toward [[South America]], then turn west along the Venezuelan coast. The islands' dominant Indigenous people were the Kalinago, while the [[Greater Antilles]] were settled by peoples including the [[Taíno]]. The boundary between them is known as the "poison arrow curtain," named after the Kalinago's favored weapon against Europeans who came to conquer the islands in the 16th century. The archipelago is politically divided into eight sovereign states, all formerly part of the British Empire, and 17 non-sovereign dependencies of France, the Netherlands, the United Kingdom, the United States, or Venezuela. Economies rely on tourism, international financial services, and limited agriculture, and hurricanes and volcanic eruptions are recurrent hazards.

Archipelago in [[Indonesia]] and Timor Leste, also known as the Nusa Tenggara Islands. They form part of the Sunda Arc, a volcanic arc formed by subduction along the Sunda Trench, and most lie in the Wallacea region. The northern archipelago, including [[Bali]], Lombok, Sumbawa, and Flores, is volcanic in origin, and Mount Rinjani on Lombok is still active. The southern islands, including Sumba and [[Timor]], are non-volcanic. The northern group began forming during the [[Pliocene]], about 15 million years ago, from the collision of the Australian and Asian plates. The Wallace Line passes between Bali and Lombok, and the islands to the east blend Asian and Australasian wildlife. Limited movement between islands has produced a high rate of localized species, most famously the [[Komodo dragon]]. The islands have the driest climate in Indonesia. The population was 3,460,059 in 1930, and today over 17 million people live on the islands.

Structured period of time in which learning is intended to occur. One or more [[Student|students]], also called pupils or learners, are taught by a [[Teacher|teacher]] or instructor. A lesson may be a section of a textbook or, more often, a short period in which learners are taught a subject or skill, usually in a classroom. Teachers typically follow a lesson plan, and a group of lessons may be linked in a unit plan. Lessons can be delivered through film strips, audio and video tapes, television, and podcasts, and video conferencing and virtual learning environments allow interactive lessons for students in different places. In a wider sense, a lesson is an insight gained by a [[Learning|learner]] into unfamiliar subject matter, planned or accidental. The phrase "to teach someone a lesson" means to punish or scold a person for a mistake. When [[Education|education]] is combined with [[Entertainment|entertainment]], the result is called edutainment.

Method of execution involving the injection of drugs into the bloodstream, mainly used for [[Capital punishment]]. It typically combines a [[Barbiturate]], a paralytic, and [[Potassium chloride]], causing unconsciousness, cessation of breathing, and [[Cardiac arrest]]. Developed in the United States, where it is now the most common form of legal execution, it was first used by Nazi Germany during World War II. Oklahoma became the first U.S. state to approve it, in 1977. Critics call it cruel and unusual, citing untrained personnel and cases in which condemned people were injected with paralytics and a cardiac arrest-inducing agent while still conscious, a technique compared to [[Torture]].

Grapheme in a writing system that generally corresponds to a [[Phoneme|phoneme]], the smallest functional unit of speech, though one-to-one correspondence is rare. A single phoneme may be written with several letters, such as the English digraphs *ch*, *sh*, and *th*. An [[Alphabet|alphabet]] is a writing system that uses letters. Letter names vary by language: Z is called zed in most of the English-speaking world and zee in the United States. Letters also function as numerals, as in [[Roman numerals]]. Phonograms, graphic symbols of sounds, appeared in Ancient Egypt and Ancient China by c. 3000 BCE. The first consonantal alphabet emerged around c. 1800 BCE, developed by Semitic workers in Egypt. The [[Phoenician alphabet|Phoenician]] alphabet, with 22 letters, spread through trade. The Greek alphabet was the first to assign letters to vowels, and the Etruscans and Romans derived the [[Latin alphabet|Latin alphabet]], now the most widely used.

Annual plant (*Lactuca sativa*) of the family [[Asteraceae]], grown mostly as a leaf vegetable. Its leaves are most often eaten raw in green [[Salad|salads]], and it is also used in sandwiches, wraps, soups, and grilled dishes. Celtuce, a variety grown for its stems, is eaten raw or cooked. Ancient Egyptians transformed it from a plant grown for oil from its seeds into a food crop grown for its leaves. The Romans named it *lactuca*, from the milky latex exuded by cut stems, and the English word derives from that name. Many varieties were developed in Europe in the 16th through 18th centuries. [[Carl Linnaeus]] first described the species in 1753. In 2023, world production of lettuce and [[Chicory|chicory]] was 28 million metric tons, led by China with 53% of the total. Contaminated lettuce is a common source of outbreaks of [[Salmonella]] and E. coli.

Group of blood cancers that usually begin in the bone marrow and produce high numbers of abnormal blood cells, called blasts. Symptoms may include bleeding and bruising, bone pain, fatigue, fever, and frequent infections, and diagnosis is typically made by [[Blood test|blood tests]] or bone marrow biopsy. Risk factors include smoking, ionizing radiation, petrochemicals such as [[Benzene]], prior [[Chemotherapy]], and [[Down syndrome]]. The four main types are acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL), acute myeloid leukemia (AML), chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL), and chronic myeloid leukemia (CML). Acute forms require immediate treatment and are the most common in children, with ALL accounting for three-quarters of childhood cases. Treatment may combine chemotherapy, [[Radiation therapy]], targeted therapy, and bone marrow transplant. The five-year survival rate was 69% in the United States from 2016 to 2022. In 2015, leukemia was present in 2.3 million people worldwide and caused 353,500 deaths.

Russian and Soviet psychologist best known for research on children's psychological development and for cultural-historical activity theory. He argued that human mental abilities are not biologically determined but are created and shaped by language and tools used in social interaction. He saw mediation through cultural tools as the path to development, through a process of interiorization. His concept of the zone of proximal development is the gap between a child's current level and the level the child can reach with help from others. He regarded play as a crucial aspect of development. His books and research were banned in the [[Soviet Union]] until the death of [[Joseph Stalin]] in 1953, and a first collection of major texts was published in 1956. A 2002 survey ranked him the 83rd most cited psychologist of the 20th century.

Soviet football goalkeeper, widely regarded as the greatest in the sport's history. He is the only goalkeeper to win the Ballon d'Or, in 1963. He revolutionized the position by commanding his defense and running out to meet attackers. He wore a kit that appeared black but was very dark blue, earning the nicknames the Black Spider and the Black Panther. He appeared in three [[FIFA World Cup|World Cups]] from 1958 to 1966, and won gold at the 1956 Olympic football tournament and the 1960 [[UEFA European Championship|European Championships]]. According to [[FIFA]], he saved over 150 penalty kicks. He was deputy chairman of the Football Federation of the [[Soviet Union]].

Subregion of [[West Asia]] along the eastern Mediterranean, forming part of the [[Middle East]]. In its narrowest sense, used in archaeology, it covers Cyprus and the land bordering the Levantine Sea, including [[Syria]], [[Lebanon]], [[Jordan]], Palestine, Israel, and southern Cilicia in Turkey. In its widest historical sense, it extended from Greece to Egypt and Cyrenaica. The word derives from the Italian *levante*, meaning "rising," a reference to the sunrise. In 1581, England set up the Levant Company to trade with the [[Ottoman Empire]]. After World War I, the French mandate over Syria and Lebanon was called the Levant States, and the term came to refer to modern Syria, Lebanon, Palestine, Israel, Jordan, and Cyprus. Several dictionaries consider the term archaic, though archaeologists still speak of Levantine archaeology.

Elevated ridge or embankment alongside a river or coastline, built to protect adjoining land from flooding. Also called a dike, dyke, floodbank, or stop bank, it is usually earthen. Natural levees form when sediment settles on the banks of a [[Floodplain]] during floods, creating a ridge that increases the channel's capacity. Artificial levees are built from fill to regulate water levels, though in some circumstances they damage the environment. Ancient civilizations in the Indus Valley, [[Ancient Egypt]], [[Mesopotamia]], and [[China]] all built levees. Levee failures can cause major disasters, such as the 2005 failures in Greater [[New Orleans]] during [[Hurricane Katrina]]. The word levee, favored in American English, comes from French and was recorded in New Orleans a few years after the city's founding in 1718. The modern word dike most likely derives from Dutch *dijk*.

Work of [[Political philosophy|political philosophy]] by English thinker [[Thomas Hobbes]], published in 1651. Its full title is *Leviathan, or The Matter, Forme and Power of a Commonwealth Ecclesiasticall and Civil*. Written during the [[English Civil War]], it is regarded as one of the earliest and most influential works of social contract theory. Hobbes argues that civil war and the "nasty, brutish and short" state of nature could be avoided only through a strong, undivided government under an absolute [[Sovereignty|sovereign]]. The title alludes to the [[Leviathan]] sea serpent of the [[Hebrew Bible]]. The frontispiece, by Abraham Bosse, shows a giant crowned figure whose torso is composed of more than 300 people. Royalists condemned the book for elevating the state over monarchy, and clergy for bordering on atheism.

Giant sea serpent in theology and mythology. It appears in the [[Hebrew Bible]] as a metaphor for a powerful enemy, notably [[Babylon]], and in Psalms, Job, Isaiah, and Enoch. Christian theologians identified it with the [[Demon|demon]] of the deadly sin envy. In the Book of Job, it reflects the older Canaanite Lotan, a monster defeated by the god Baal Hadad. Some 19th-century scholars interpreted it as a [[Crocodile|crocodile]], and the word later came to mean a great [[Whale|whale]] and sea monsters in general. Thomas Hobbes used the figure in his [[Leviathan (Hobbes book)|Leviathan]] as a metaphor for the omnipotence of the state.

Pen name of Charles Lutwidge Dodgson, English author, poet, mathematician, and photographer. His best-known works are *Alice's Adventures in Wonderland* (1865) and its sequel *Through the Looking-Glass* (1871), important examples of Victorian literature. His poems "Jabberwocky" (1871) and *The Hunting of the Snark* (1876) are classified as literary nonsense. Carroll came from a family of high-church Anglicans and lived most of his life at [[University of Oxford|Christ Church, Oxford]], where he taught mathematics from 1855 to 1881 and served as an Anglican deacon. He published on [[Mathematical logic]], and some of Alice's wonderland logic reflects that work. Alice Liddell, daughter of the dean of Christ Church, is widely identified as the inspiration for Alice, though Carroll always denied this. He was an accomplished photographer from 1856, known for portraits of children, and he created the word-ladder puzzle "Doublets," published in *Vanity Fair* from 1879 to 1881.

British racing driver who competes in [[Formula One]] for [[Scuderia Ferrari|Ferrari]]. He has won a joint-record seven world drivers' championships, tied with [[Michael Schumacher]], and holds the record for most podium finishes (209). Born in Stevenage, he joined the [[McLaren]] young driver program in 1998 and won his first title with McLaren in 2008. He then drove for Mercedes, winning titles in 2014, 2015, and 2017 to 2020. He signed for Ferrari in 2025. He was knighted by [[Elizabeth II]] and is an advocate for racial justice and greater diversity in motorsport.

American expedition, 1804–06, to explore the western territory acquired in the [[Louisiana Purchase]]. Also called the Corps of Discovery Expedition, it was commissioned by President [[Thomas Jefferson]] shortly after the Louisiana Purchase of 1803 and led by Captain Meriwether Lewis and Second Lieutenant William Clark. Clark, with 30 others, left Camp Dubois in Illinois on May 14, 1804, and went up the [[Missouri River]]. The corps crossed the Continental Divide, reached the [[Pacific Ocean]] in 1805, and began the return voyage from Fort Clatsop, Oregon, on March 23, 1806. Jefferson sought a practical water route to the Pacific, a declaration of U.S. sovereignty over Native American lands, and an American presence before European powers could claim the territory. The expedition also documented the West's biodiversity, topography, and geography and aimed to build trade relations with Native American tribes.
